title: State of the art for scheduling and analyzing self-suspending sporadic real-time tasks

extraction.paper_name: State of the Art for Scheduling and Analyzing Self-Suspending Sporadic Real-Time Tasks
extraction.paper_description: A survey paper summarizing task models (dynamic, segmented, hybrid) and schedulability tests for self-suspending tasks on uniprocessor systems, focusing on fixed-priority and EDF scheduling.

formal_description.statement: A sporadic self-suspending task tau_i is characterized by (C_i, T_i, D_i, S_i)
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the basic parameters for a self-suspending task.

informal_sketch.intuition: Extends the standard sporadic task model by adding a parameter for the maximum time a task can spend suspended (waiting for I/O, offloading, etc.).
steps: A task tau_i releases jobs at least T_i time units apart
Each job requires up to C_i execution time
Each job must finish within D_i of its release
Each job can suspend for a total of S_i time
key_insights: Self-suspension allows the processor to be idle or run lower-priority tasks while the current task waits.

formal_description.statement: Dynamic Self-Suspension Model: A job of tau_i can suspend itself at any moment as long as the total suspension time does not exceed S_i
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a flexible but potentially pessimistic suspension model.

informal_sketch.intuition: The task can suspend 'arbitrarily often' and for any duration, provided the sum of all suspension durations in one job is <= S_i.
steps: Job starts execution
At any point, it can stop and enter suspension
It can resume and suspend again multiple times
Total suspension time sum <= S_i
key_insights: High flexibility for system designers but harder to analyze accurately.

formal_description.statement: Segmented Self-Suspension Model: tau_i = (C_i_1, S_i_1, C_i_2, S_i_2, ..., S_i_mi_minus_1, C_i_mi)

variables.C_i_j: Execution time of the j-th computation segment
variables.S_i_j: Duration of the j-th suspension interval

formal_description.conclusion: Defines a restrictive but accurate suspension model with fixed patterns.

informal_sketch.intuition: The task follows a strict sequence of execution and suspension phases.
steps: Execute C_i_1
Suspend for S_i_1
Execute C_i_2
Repeat until C_i_mi is finished
key_insights: More information allows for tighter schedulability analysis compared to the dynamic model.

formal_description.statement: B_k = S_k + sum_{tau_i in hp_k} min(S_i, C_i)

variables.hp_k: Set of tasks with higher priority than k

formal_description.conclusion: Calculates the effective blocking time caused by self-suspensions.

informal_sketch.intuition: Suspensions in higher-priority tasks can be modeled as blocking time for the task under analysis.
steps: Start with the task's own suspension time S_k
For each higher priority task, add the minimum of its execution or suspension time
This sum represents the maximum delay tau_k can suffer due to suspension-induced priority inversion
key_insights: Treating suspension as blocking is a common technique to reuse standard response time analysis.

formal_description.statement: exists t | 0 < t <= D_k, S_k + C_k + sum_{tau_i in hp_k} ceil(t / T_i) * (C_i + S_i) <= t
formal_description.conclusion: Task tau_k is schedulable (Suspension as Computation)

informal_sketch.intuition: Treat all suspension time as if it were execution time.
steps: For every task, redefine execution time as C_i_prime = C_i + S_i
Apply standard Response Time Analysis (RTA)
If the task finishes before D_k, it is schedulable
key_insights: Simplest but most pessimistic test; assumes tasks use the CPU even when suspended.

formal_description.statement: exists t | 0 < t <= D_k, C_k + B_k + sum_{tau_i in hp_k} ceil(t / T_i) * C_i <= t
formal_description.conclusion: Task tau_k is schedulable (Suspension as Blocking)

informal_sketch.intuition: Uses the blocking term B_k to account for suspensions without inflating the execution time of every higher-priority job instance.
steps: Calculate B_k using Claim 1
Check the workload equation including B_k
If any t satisfies the inequality, the task is schedulable
key_insights: Generally tighter than Theorem 1 because S_i is only added once (as part of B_k) rather than for every job release.

formal_description.statement: exists t | 0 < t <= D_k, S_k + C_k + sum_{tau_i in hp_k} ceil((t + D_i - C_i) / T_i) * C_i <= t

variables.D_i: Deadline of higher priority task i
variables.C_i: Execution of higher priority task i

formal_description.conclusion: Task tau_k is schedulable (Suspension as Jitter)

informal_sketch.intuition: Models the interference of higher-priority tasks by assuming they can have a release jitter equal to their maximum possible response time (D_i - C_i).
steps: For each higher priority task, calculate jitter J_i = D_i - C_i
Add this jitter to the release time in the workload calculation
Check if tau_k completes within D_k
key_insights: Uses the worst-case delay a higher-priority task can cause by finishing late and then releasing its next job immediately.

formal_description.statement: exists t | 0 < t <= D_k, S_k + C_k + sum_{i=1}^{k-1} ceil((t + Q_y_i + (1 - y_i)*(D_i - C_i)) / T_i) * C_i <= t
assumptions: Tasks indexed 1 to k-1 by priority
formal_description.conclusion: Task tau_k is schedulable (Tightest combined test)

informal_sketch.intuition: A hybrid approach that chooses between modeling higher-priority suspension as jitter or as a blocking-like term (Q_y_i) for each task to find the tightest bound.
steps: Define a vector y where each element is 0 or 1
Calculate Q_y_i as the sum of suspensions of lower-priority tasks (relative to i) that are treated as blocking
Evaluate the workload equation
The paper suggests specific heuristics for choosing y_i (e.g., y_i=1 if S_i <= C_i)
key_insights: This theorem dominates Theorems 3 and 4 by allowing a per-task choice of the most efficient modeling method.

formal_description.statement: (C_k + S_k) / T_k + 2 * sum_{tau_i in hp_k} (C_i / T_i) + 1 <= 3
formal_description.conclusion: Task tau_k is schedulable (Constant-time test based on Thm 1)

informal_sketch.intuition: A simplified utilization-based check for RM scheduling that incorporates suspension time by treating it as computation.
steps: Calculate utilization of higher priority tasks
Add the normalized execution and suspension of the task under analysis
Check against the derived bound (3 in this case)
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def test_theorem_6(tau_k, hp_tasks):
    U_hp = sum(tau_i.C_i / tau_i.T_i for tau_i in hp_tasks)
    val = (tau_k.C_i + tau_k.S_i) / tau_k.T_k + 2 * U_hp + 1
    return val <= 3
key_insights: Provides an O(1) check if utilization sums are pre-calculated.

formal_description.statement: dbf_FRD_i(t, D_i_1) = max(dbf_1_i(t, D_i_1), dbf_2_i(t, D_i_1))

variables.dbf_1_i: floor((t + T_i - D_i_1) / T_i) * C_i_1 + floor(t / T_i) * C_i_2
variables.dbf_2_i: floor((t + D_i_1 + S_i) / T_i) * C_i_2 + floor((t + S_i) / T_i) * C_i_1
variables.D_i_1: Relative deadline assigned to the first segment

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the Demand Bound Function for a segmented task under EDF.

informal_sketch.intuition: Calculates the maximum possible execution demand of a segmented task in any time interval of length t by checking two worst-case alignment patterns.
steps: Pattern 1: The first segment C_i_1 is released at the start of the interval
Pattern 2: The second segment C_i_2 is released at the start of the interval
The DBF is the maximum demand produced by either pattern
key_insights: Essential for applying EDF analysis to segmented tasks.

formal_description.statement: sum_{tau_i in T} dbf_FRD_i(t, D_i_1) <= t, for all t >= 0
formal_description.conclusion: The task set is schedulable under FRD.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task set is schedulable under EDF if the total demand in any interval t never exceeds the available time t.
steps: Assign relative deadlines D_i_j to segments
Calculate the total DBF for all tasks
Verify the condition for all critical time points t
key_insights: Converts the self-suspension problem into a multiframe task scheduling problem.
